transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-03-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Priya Shah (Redwood AE), Daniel Cooper (Redwood SE), Alicia Gomez (Nimbus ML), Ben Carter (Nimbus Infra), Samir Patel (Nimbus Sec)
---
[00:00] Priya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Priya from Redwood, today we want to walk through the performance characteristics when you run structured function outputs and json payloads especially when you add quantization, kv cache behavior, batching and in a VPC/on-prem network environment
[00:18] Alicia: thanks, yeah we've seen some variance in latency when we ask for strict JSON mode and then do tool calls, plus our infra team is nervous about on-prem network hops
[00:28] Daniel: yeah quick note — i'll be toggling to some microbenchmarks and explain how the runtime chooses kernels, and where extra token decoding overhead comes from when you force constrained tokens for json validity
[00:40] Ben: we're testing with a 2k token context and short tool payloads, target p95 under 350ms for single-request median ideally under 200ms — is that realistic with quant+kv?
[00:55] Daniel: short answer: depends on several axes. i'll try to break them down: model size/architecture, quant profile (16/8/4-bit), batch size, kv cache hit ratio, decoding mode (beam vs sampling vs constrained), plus network placement (hosted vs vpc/onprem). there are tradeoffs.
[01:20] Samir: also SOC2 / audit concerns — when we move to Private VPC we need encrypt-in-transit plus audit logs. that impacts perf if we add TLS termination on-prem
[01:33] Priya: totally. i'll flag that Redwood Private supports customer-managed TLS/KMS and audit retention options, but performance impact depends on where TLS terminates and whether inference is co-located with the KMS calls
[01:46] Alicia: can we start with the JSON mode overhead? when we set "structured_output: json_strict" we see 30-60ms extra on average per request. what's happening
[01:58] Daniel: right — constrained decoding to enforce exact JSON tokens usually forces the decoder to consult a small validity automaton per step. on top of that, we often add token-level post-processing validation which can lead to extra synchronous checks. two sources: generation-time token filtering and synchronous post-decode reparsing and correction loops. depending on model tokenizer granularity, that can be non-trivial
[02:25] Daniel: e.g., when you require a strict JSON-close token '}' the runtime will check the token graph; if sampling temperature is non-zero that constraining reduces parallelism micro-optimizations in the decoder and prevents some kernel-level fusion — net result: 15-80ms overhead on short responses
[02:44] Ben: is that amplification worse with quant? because quant adds compute variability
[02:50] Daniel: yes for 8-bit the compute is faster on the matmul paths, but the decoder loop becomes memory-bound if you keep jumping in/out for validity checks. with 4-bit (Q4_0-style) we sometimes batch more aggressively, but the decoding tight loop can suffer due to extra dequant/packed ops — so it's nuanced
[03:10] Alicia: our primary failure mode is malformed json that breaks downstream tool calls. we need strictness but can't double latency
[03:17] Priya: a common pattern is hybrid: use relaxed constrained decoding + quick deterministic post-processor that tries to patch missing commas/quotes, then a fast schema validator in the app layer. that reduces decoder pressure and moves cheap fixes off the critical path
[03:33] Samir: that feels risky for compliance — we need auditable transformations
[03:38] Daniel: fair — you can instrument the post-processor and record diffs in audit logs. Redwood can attach a transformation provenance header on the response so you know whether the runtime modified tokens vs appended sanitizer notes
[03:52] Ben: how does KV cache interact? we rely on persistent KV state across user sessions to avoid re-priming prompts
[03:59] Daniel: KV cache helps dramatically when the repetition ratio is high — it saves early decode tokens and can drop p50 cost by 30-60%. but when you do strict constrained outputs the KV cache can change token boundaries: if a cached prefix ends mid-token for the constrained grammar, you may need to recompute a partial decode which reduces cache effectiveness
[04:22] Daniel: also in private deployments with local persistent store latency is small, but in hosted with remote KV we sometimes add 5-10ms network penalty per request for cache lookups unless you colocate cache and model runtime
[04:36] Alicia: what's the guidance for batching? we see big throughput gains but latency spikes when a batch waits
[04:43] Daniel: Redwood supports dynamic batching with latency SLOs. the general trade: larger batches increase throughput but add queuing latency. we recommend adaptive policies: small batches for p95-sensitive endpoints (batch size 1-4) and behind-the-scenes frank batching for throughput endpoints. the runtime will cap batch wait to your SLO, e.g., max_wait_ms=30
[05:05] Ben: in our perf runs we set max_wait_ms=50 and p95 ballooned — do we have a formula
[05:12] Daniel: rough model: avg_latency = compute_time_per_request + (batch_size-1)*avg_interarrival * 0.5 + scheduling_overhead. if your traffic is bursty, batching hurts p95. use request shaping or reserve dedicated capacity for low-latency routes
[05:33] Alicia: about quantization — you mentioned Q4_0 and Q8 — what's safe for structured JSON outputs
[05:40] Daniel: for many open models Q8 (8-bit) retains decoding fidelity and has lower variance. Q4 can be OK but sometimes produces tokenization drift that creates off-by-one commas or quote issues. For strict JSON, we recommend Q8 for pilot, then test Q4 on specific workloads. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload
[06:02] Priya: for private deployments we can supply a quantized binary whitelabel image if you need air-gapped
[06:09] Samir: network topology question: if we host model inside our VPC but use Redwood control plane remote, do we see extra egress on token-by-token calls during function invocation
[06:20] Daniel: function/tool calls that invoke external endpoints will produce the function payload at the end of generation, i.e., we typically send the tool payload as one object after decode finishes. but if you stream partial tokens to tools (we call that streaming-invoke) that can increase network chatter. we default to single-call function invocation to avoid token-by-token egress
[06:41] Ben: are there cases where runtime offloads pieces to the control plane and that adds latency
[06:46] Daniel: only for metadata operations (e.g., model switching, metrics) — inference path is local to the runtime worker. in Private VPC the runtime and KV can be colocated so control plane roundtrip is minimized
[06:57] Alicia: can you walk us through the microbenchmark Daniel ran earlier? you mentioned chart in the deck
[07:02] Daniel: sure — results are on the shared spreadsheet link: https://rwd/benchmarks/structured-payloads-march2026 (note: placeholder). summary: for a 350-char JSON payload, Hosted (non-quant) median: 160ms, p95: 320ms. Hosted Q8: median 125ms p95 260ms. Q4 median 110ms p95 420ms (increased variance). with strict-json constraints: add +40ms median and +80ms p95 on Q8
[07:30] Ben: that p95 jump for Q4 is concerning
[07:33] Daniel: it's variance — some tokenization edge cases cause extra retries. we also instrumented out-of-vocab sequences that cause sampling loop to fall back to full beam for a few steps which is heavy
[07:46] Priya: noted that the deck also includes kernel-level trace — i'll attach that after the call
[07:50] Alicia: what's the recommended pilot configuration to validate for us?
[07:55] Daniel: recommended pilot: Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) with a single worker type using Q8 quant, dynamic batching with max_wait_ms=25, KV cache colocated on the same host, and structured_output set to relaxed_constrained with app-level validator. Run 10k requests across your canonical prompt set to capture distribution
[08:20] Ben: what about memory footprint for Q8 vs Q4 on a 24GB GPU
[08:26] Daniel: Q8 reduces memory ~40% relative to fp16, Q4 reduces ~60%. On 24GB you can host larger models with Q4 but you must watch for per-request scratch buffers during decoding
[08:40] Samir: our compliance requires we never call external KMS during inference. can you support local HSM
[08:46] Priya: yes Redwood Private supports HSM/KMS integrations on-prem. we can run with customer-managed keys and we have an audit mode that logs key usage events
[08:56] Alicia: back to structured outputs — is there an alternate approach like using schema-guided prompts instead of strict decoding
[09:03] Daniel: schema-guided prompts are often a good compromise: instruct model with a synthetic schema and use temperature=0 deterministic decode with heuristics. it avoids runtime token-level automata but isn't 100% reliable. mixing prompt engineering, light constrained filtering and app-level validation usually gives best latency-accuracy tradeoff
[09:24] Ben: a question on tracing: we need per-token latency breakdown for p99 investigations
[09:29] Daniel: Redwood Console supports token-level latency breakdown when you enable tracing for the route. there's a cost owing to increased telemetry, but it's invaluable for debugging spikes. we can sample 1% of traffic for full traces
[09:44] Alicia: can Console show quantization-specific heatmaps
[09:48] Daniel: yes — we surface per-model/per-quant-profile histograms, batch impact, and KV hit rates
[09:55] Priya: i want to call out a corner case — tool-calling combined with streaming: if you stream as you generate and simultaneously call a tool to enrich partial payloads, you can get higher throughput but it's complex and can cause tail latency due to backpressure
[10:12] Ben: do you have heuristics when streaming-invoke is worth it
[10:16] Daniel: yes: use streaming-invoke when tool latency is very low and tool enrichments significantly reduce remaining decode length. otherwise batch the tool calls at the end
[10:27] Alicia: we also run in k8s on-prem with node-level NUMA issues; any advice to reduce jitter
[10:33] Daniel: pinning threads, setting CPU governor, and isolating interrupts helps. also GPU topology: avoid colocating multiple worker types on same GPU if they have different memory patterns. Redwood's dedicated nodes can be provisioned with NUMA-aware placement
[10:50] Ben: curious on cost tradeoffs — if we choose Dedicated Q8 vs Private Q4 what is typical cost multiplier
[10:56] Priya: ballpark — Dedicated Q8 is cheaper than Private Q4 because Private includes additional infra & support. but model memory compression can let Q4 run on fewer GPUs lowering cloud compute. we'll share a comparative cost calc in the SOW
[11:11] Alicia: can we get examples of tokenization failures that caused JSON breakage
[11:15] Daniel: yes here's a recorded example in the spreadsheet — the model emitted '"name": John' with unquoted value, tokenizer split 'John' oddly as two tokens and the constrained automaton rejected the closing brace causing fallback. that was fixed by prompt hinting and slight tokenizer normalization
[11:35] Ben: good to know. what's the recommended testing matrix for us
[11:40] Daniel: test matrix: run each quant profile (fp16/Q8/Q4), two batch configs (1 and 8), structured mode options (none/relaxed/strict), KV hit ratios (cold/30%/70%/90%), and network topologies (hosted, dedicated-colocated, private-vpc). collect median/p95/p99, error rates, malformed JSON rate
[12:05] Priya: next steps recap — we'll run the 10k pilot in Dedicated Q8 and share results; customer to provide prompts. we'll also schedule a follow-up deep-dive for p99 root cause if needed
[12:17] Alicia: sounds good. Samir — any security blockers to proceed?
[12:21] Samir: need to review SOW and ensure audit logging meets our retention policy; otherwise no blockers
[12:27] Ben: quick question — what about token streaming cost accounting for billing
[12:31] Priya: billing is per-token generated; streaming doesn't change tokens counted but we can show per-route token breakdowns in Console
[12:39] Daniel: one more note — if you plan to use large tool payloads consider compressing function args; function payload size affects total tokens and latency
[12:47] Alicia: can you add a baseline with compressed payloads
[12:49] Daniel: yes i'll add gzip comparisons in the spreadsheet
[12:52] Priya: ok wrapping up, i'll send slides, the benchmark link, and SOW draft. any last q's
[12:58] Ben: none here
[13:00] Alicia: thanks all
[13:02] Samir: thanks
---
Summary:
- Pilot recommended: Dedicated Q8, colocated KV, relaxed constrained JSON + app-layer validator
- Strict JSON adds measurable decode overhead; Q4 increases variance and risk of malformed outputs
- Batching must be tuned to traffic patterns; use max_wait_ms and dynamic batching or dedicated capacity for p95-sensitive endpoints
- Private VPC/HSM supported, but auditing and TLS termination design impacts latency
